title: GERD: Treat the Syndrome, Investigate the Alarm Feature
bottomLine: Typical reflux without alarm features can often be managed clinically with lifestyle measures and an appropriate acid-suppression trial. Dysphagia, bleeding, anemia, weight loss, persistent vomiting or an atypical/refractory course changes the pathway to diagnostic evaluation rather than indefinite empiric PPI escalation.
recognize: Heartburn and regurgitation are typical symptoms, while cough/chest/throat complaints are less specific and need a broader differential.
Pregnancy and obesity can increase reflux symptoms without changing the need to investigate red flags.
differentiate: Cardiac ischemia, peptic ulcer, biliary disease and eosinophilic esophagitis can mimic reflux symptoms.
Dysphagia is not simply 'severe GERD' and deserves structural/motility evaluation.
assessment: Assess symptom pattern, meals/position, dysphagia/odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss, NSAIDs, tobacco/alcohol, pregnancy and medication triggers.
workup: Use endoscopy or further reflux/motility testing for alarm features, refractory symptoms or diagnostic uncertainty rather than routinely for every typical presentation.
Do not use repeated imaging as a substitute for appropriate endoscopic evaluation when alarms are present.
management: Use weight/meal/tobacco/alcohol measures when relevant and an evidence-based PPI or other acid-suppression strategy.
Use the lowest effective long-term acid suppression when ongoing therapy is truly indicated and reassess chronic use periodically.
medicationSafety: PPIs are generally effective and safe when indicated, but chronic therapy should have a documented indication and periodic review rather than automatic continuation.
Review interacting drugs and magnesium/B12/renal concerns when the clinical context makes them relevant rather than ordering universal monitoring.
redFlags: Severe chest pain with cardiac concern
counselling: Explain that symptom improvement supports treatment response but does not erase alarm features.
Teach when new dysphagia, bleeding or weight loss requires prompt reassessment.
followUp: Reassess after a defined treatment trial and step down/deprescribe when appropriate; persistent or relapsing alarm symptoms require endoscopic/specialty evaluation.
examTrap: Increasing the PPI indefinitely for progressive dysphagia instead of changing to a diagnostic pathway.
oneLinePearl: Typical reflux can be treated empirically; alarm symptoms must be explained.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology GERD/dyspepsia practice resources

title: Peptic Ulcer and H. pylori: Treat the Cause and Prove Eradication
bottomLine: Peptic ulcer disease management requires identifying H. pylori, NSAID/aspirin exposure and complication risk. If H. pylori is treated, confirm eradication with an appropriate test after therapy; symptom improvement alone does not prove cure.
recognize: Epigastric pain/dyspepsia can occur, but ulcer bleeding may present with melena, hematemesis, anemia or syncope.
NSAIDs and H. pylori are major modifiable causes and can coexist.
differentiate: Noninvasive H. pylori testing is appropriate in selected uncomplicated dyspepsia; alarm features or ulcer complications may require endoscopy.
Serology can remain positive after prior infection and is not the preferred eradication-confirmation test.
assessment: Review NSAIDs/aspirin, anticoagulants, prior ulcer/bleed, H. pylori history, smoking, anemia symptoms, weight loss and family/upper-GI cancer risk.
workup: Use urea breath or stool antigen testing when appropriate and account for medications that can reduce test sensitivity.
Use endoscopy urgently or electively according to bleeding/alarm/severity context.
management: Use current Canadian/local H. pylori eradication regimens informed by prior antibiotic exposure/resistance context and provide acid suppression as indicated.
Stop/reduce ulcerogenic drugs when possible or add gastroprotection when they must continue.
medicationSafety: Avoid outdated empiric regimens when local resistance makes them unreliable.
Bismuth/antibiotic/PPI regimens have interaction, adherence and pregnancy considerations that require product-specific review.
counselling: Explain the importance of completing eradication therapy and returning for test-of-cure even if symptoms disappear.
followUp: Confirm H. pylori eradication at the appropriate interval and reassess ongoing NSAID/aspirin need and recurrent symptoms.
examTrap: Assuming H. pylori is eradicated because the patient feels better after therapy.
oneLinePearl: Treat H. pylori, then test that it is gone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology H. pylori/dyspepsia resources

title: Dyspepsia: Risk-Stratify Before Endoscopy or Long-Term Medication
bottomLine: Dyspepsia is an upper-GI symptom syndrome, not a diagnosis of ulcer disease. Assess alarm/cancer risk, NSAIDs and H. pylori probability, then choose test-and-treat, acid suppression or endoscopy based on age/risk/context rather than sending every patient directly to imaging or scope.
recognize: Postprandial fullness, early satiety and epigastric pain/burning are common dyspeptic symptoms.
Functional dyspepsia is diagnosed after appropriate evaluation excludes structural disease when indicated.
differentiate: GERD is dominated by reflux symptoms; biliary/pancreatic disease and cardiac ischemia can mimic upper abdominal discomfort.
Alarm features and cancer risk change the threshold for endoscopy.
assessment: Assess duration, weight loss, vomiting, dysphagia, anemia/bleeding, family history, NSAIDs, H. pylori history, age/risk and pregnancy.
workup: Use noninvasive H. pylori testing when appropriate and endoscopy when alarm/risk/refractory context warrants it.
Avoid indiscriminate abdominal imaging for uncomplicated dyspepsia without a targeted indication.
management: Treat H. pylori when present, use a defined PPI trial when appropriate and address NSAID/other contributors.
Persistent functional dyspepsia may require dietary, neuromodulator or GI strategies after appropriate evaluation.
medicationSafety: Long-term acid suppression should have a reason and review plan.
Avoid repeated NSAID exposure in ulcer-risk patients without reassessing necessity/gastroprotection.
counselling: Explain that dyspepsia can be functional after important structural disease is excluded and that this does not make symptoms imaginary.
followUp: Reassess response after a defined trial and escalate diagnostic evaluation when the pattern changes or fails to improve appropriately.
examTrap: Ordering CT for routine uncomplicated dyspepsia instead of first addressing H. pylori, NSAIDs and alarm features.
oneLinePearl: Dyspepsia is a risk-stratification problem before it is a procedure problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology dyspepsia guidance

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Confirm Inflammation, Define Extent, Monitor Complications
bottomLine: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis require objective evidence of chronic intestinal inflammation and disease extent. Separate IBD from infection and IBS, assess severity/complications, and use steroid-sparing maintenance strategies with appropriate infection/vaccine/therapy monitoring rather than repeated empiric steroids.
recognize: Chronic diarrhea, blood, urgency, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia and extraintestinal manifestations can occur.
Crohn disease may be transmural/segmental with fistula/stricture; ulcerative colitis is continuous colonic mucosal disease.
differentiate: IBS does not cause objective intestinal inflammation, anemia or weight loss.
C. difficile and other infection can mimic or complicate IBD flares and should be considered before escalation of immunosuppression.
assessment: Assess stool frequency/blood, pain, fever, hydration, weight, perianal disease, extraintestinal symptoms, smoking, pregnancy, current biologic/immunosuppressive therapy and infection risk.
workup: Use CBC/chemistry/inflammatory markers and stool testing where indicated plus endoscopy/imaging to establish and phenotype disease.
Use fecal calprotectin when it answers an inflammation/monitoring question rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis.
management: Treat acute and maintenance disease according to location/severity using current Canadian GI guidance and steroid-sparing therapy.
Hospitalize severe colitis, obstruction, abscess, sepsis or major dehydration and involve gastroenterology/surgery early.
medicationSafety: Before biologic/immunomodulator therapy, follow current infection-screening and vaccination guidance.
Repeated systemic corticosteroids are not acceptable maintenance therapy and accumulate infection, bone, glucose and adrenal risk.
counselling: Discuss smoking cessation in Crohn disease, medication adherence, vaccination, pregnancy planning and colon-cancer surveillance.
followUp: Track symptoms plus objective inflammation and therapy toxicity; surveillance colonoscopy depends on disease duration/extent/risk.
examTrap: Calling chronic diarrhea IBS despite anemia/weight loss and objective inflammation—or giving repeated prednisone bursts without a maintenance strategy.
oneLinePearl: IBD needs proof of inflammation and a steroid-sparing long-term plan.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology current IBD guideline library

title: IBS: Make a Positive Diagnosis After Checking the Alarm Features
bottomLine: IBS is a disorder of gut–brain interaction diagnosed from a compatible chronic symptom pattern after limited targeted evaluation and absence of concerning alarms. It should not become a label that prevents reevaluation when bleeding, anemia, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, fever or a major pattern change appears.
recognize: Recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and change in stool frequency/form is typical.
Symptoms can be severe despite normal routine testing and are not explained by 'stress' alone.
differentiate: IBD, celiac disease, colorectal disease, microscopic colitis, medication effects and infection can mimic IBS.
Objective inflammation, blood loss and progressive weight loss are not routine IBS features.
assessment: Assess stool pattern, pain relationship, bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, weight, family history, diet, medications, anxiety/depression and prior testing.
workup: Use targeted CBC/celiac and inflammatory/stool testing when the phenotype/risk supports it rather than exhaustive exclusion panels.
Colonoscopy is based on age/risk/alarm/screening indications, not IBS symptoms alone.
management: Use subtype-specific dietary, fibre, antispasmodic, bowel-regulating and gut–brain therapies with shared decision-making.
Avoid unnecessarily restrictive diets without dietitian support when nutritional risk is present.
medicationSafety: Monitor constipation/diarrhea and anticholinergic/sedating adverse effects of symptom-directed agents.
Avoid chronic opioid treatment for IBS pain because it can worsen bowel dysfunction and dependence risk.
counselling: Validate symptoms as a real gut–brain disorder and explain the positive diagnostic approach rather than implying 'nothing is wrong'.
followUp: Track function and symptom response and reconsider the diagnosis when alarms or a major change appears.
examTrap: Ordering repeated colonoscopies for stable IBS with no alarm features—or refusing to reconsider IBS when new anemia develops.
oneLinePearl: IBS is a positive pattern diagnosis, but new alarm features reopen the differential.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology IBS guideline/resources

title: Celiac Disease: Test While Gluten Is Still in the Diet
bottomLine: Celiac disease requires appropriate serologic and, when indicated, histologic confirmation while the patient is consuming gluten. Starting a gluten-free diet before diagnostic testing can make results falsely reassuring and complicate lifelong dietary treatment decisions.
recognize: Diarrhea, iron deficiency, weight loss, bloating, osteoporosis, infertility and extraintestinal symptoms can occur; some patients are minimally symptomatic.
Risk is higher with first-degree family history and selected autoimmune/genetic conditions.
differentiate: Non-celiac gluten sensitivity and wheat allergy are distinct from autoimmune celiac disease.
IBS-like symptoms do not exclude celiac disease when risk features are present.
assessment: Assess gluten exposure, diarrhea/weight, iron/bone/nutrient issues, family/autoimmune history and whether a gluten-free diet has already started.
workup: Use tissue-transglutaminase IgA with total IgA in most appropriate patients and alternate serology when IgA deficient; refer for endoscopic biopsy according to age/context and current guidance.
Do not use HLA testing as routine first-line diagnosis; it is most useful in selected discordant cases.
management: Use a strict lifelong gluten-free diet after diagnosis with dietitian support and correction of nutritional deficiencies.
Refractory symptoms require assessment for ongoing gluten exposure, alternate diagnoses or complications rather than assuming treatment failure.
medicationSafety: Review medications/supplements for gluten exposure only when clinically relevant rather than creating avoidable medication fear.
Avoid prolonged empiric restriction in an unconfirmed patient without nutritional support.
counselling: Explain why testing before gluten elimination matters and connect the patient with reliable dietitian/celiac resources.
followUp: Track symptoms, nutritional deficiencies and serologic response according to current celiac follow-up guidance.
examTrap: Telling a patient to stop gluten before serologic/endoscopic testing and then using negative tests to rule out celiac disease.
oneLinePearl: For celiac diagnosis, keep gluten in until the testing question is answered.
sourceBasis: Canadian Celiac Association / Canadian gastroenterology diagnostic resources

title: Hepatitis B and C: Define Active Infection, Stage Liver Risk, Link to Curative or Suppressive Care
bottomLine: HBV and HCV require different interpretation. HCV antibody shows exposure and HCV RNA confirms active infection; HBV uses a serologic/viral-load pattern to define infection phase and treatment need. Both require fibrosis/liver-risk assessment, vaccination/coinfection counselling and linkage to current Canadian antiviral pathways.
recognize: Chronic viral hepatitis may be asymptomatic despite fibrosis progression.
Pregnancy changes HBV transmission-prevention and antiviral decisions.
differentiate: HCV antibody alone does not prove active infection after spontaneous clearance or cure.
HBsAg, anti-HBc and anti-HBs answer different HBV questions and should be interpreted together.
assessment: Assess prior testing/treatment, injection/sexual/blood exposure, country of origin, alcohol, pregnancy, HIV risk, medications and liver-decompensation symptoms.
workup: Confirm active HCV with RNA and stage liver disease; use current HBV serology, HBV DNA, ALT and fibrosis assessment to define management.
Screen for relevant coinfections and hepatocellular-carcinoma surveillance need according to current Canadian guidance.
management: Link active HCV to direct-acting antiviral treatment unless a specific contraindication/barrier requires specialist planning.
Treat/suppress HBV according to current CASL/AMMI criteria and pregnancy/perinatal prevention pathways.
medicationSafety: Review antiviral drug interactions and renal/hepatic context.
Stopping HBV-active therapy can cause flare in selected patients and must follow the treatment plan.
redFlags: Pregnancy with high-risk HBV transmission context
counselling: Explain HCV cure vs HBV suppression, transmission prevention and the role of vaccination for susceptible contacts/hepatitis A/B as appropriate.
followUp: Confirm HCV virologic response/cure and continue liver surveillance when advanced fibrosis remains; HBV follow-up tracks viral/liver activity and HCC risk.
examTrap: Calling a positive HCV antibody active hepatitis C without RNA confirmation—or treating one HBV serology marker in isolation.
oneLinePearl: For HCV, antibody means exposed and RNA means active; HBV requires the whole serologic/viral pattern.
sourceBasis: CASL/AMMI Canada 2025 chronic hepatitis B guidance
PHAC hepatitis C health-professional resources and Canadian treatment pathways

title: Metabolic Fatty Liver Disease: Fibrosis Risk Matters More Than the ALT
bottomLine: Metabolic steatotic liver disease is common and aminotransferases can be normal despite important fibrosis. The NP priority is cardiometabolic treatment plus noninvasive fibrosis-risk assessment and referral of higher-risk disease—not repeated ALT monitoring as a proxy for liver outcome.
recognize: Obesity, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia and hypertension increase risk.
Normal AST/ALT does not exclude advanced fibrosis.
differentiate: Alcohol, viral hepatitis, medications and other chronic liver diseases can coexist and should be assessed rather than assuming all steatosis is metabolic.
Simple steatosis and advanced fibrotic disease have very different prognoses.
assessment: Assess alcohol, metabolic risk, medications, viral risk, liver symptoms and signs of advanced disease.
workup: Use validated noninvasive fibrosis tools and elastography/referral pathways when risk is elevated; do not rely on ultrasound steatosis or ALT alone to stage fibrosis.
management: Treat weight-related disease, diabetes, lipids, BP and cardiovascular risk using evidence-based therapies; encourage sustainable nutrition/activity strategies.
Refer suspected advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis and manage cirrhosis complications/surveillance appropriately.
medicationSafety: Statins are not routinely withheld solely because of stable fatty liver and are often important for cardiovascular risk.
Review hepatotoxic drugs based on actual liver disease severity rather than a blanket prohibition.
counselling: Use non-stigmatizing metabolic-disease language and explain that cardiovascular risk is a major health priority alongside liver fibrosis.
followUp: Track metabolic outcomes and repeat fibrosis-risk assessment at a clinically appropriate interval rather than serial ALT alone.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with diabetes because ALT is normal despite a high fibrosis-risk profile.
oneLinePearl: In fatty liver disease, fibrosis risk—not enzyme height—drives liver prognosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian hepatology metabolic liver disease practice resources

title: Alcohol-Related Liver Disease: Stage the Liver and Treat the Alcohol Use Disorder
bottomLine: Alcohol-related liver disease care requires two linked diagnoses: the severity/complications of liver disease and the alcohol-use pattern. Do not reduce care to 'stop drinking'; assess withdrawal risk, nutrition, fibrosis/decompensation and offer evidence-based AUD treatment in a non-stigmatizing way.
recognize: Steatosis, hepatitis and cirrhosis can occur across a spectrum; aminotransferase pattern alone does not stage severity.
Jaundice, coagulopathy, ascites, encephalopathy and infection signal potentially severe disease.
differentiate: Other liver disease can coexist; do not attribute every abnormal liver test to alcohol without appropriate evaluation.
Alcohol withdrawal risk is separate from liver severity and may require monitored treatment.
assessment: Use a nonjudgmental alcohol history including quantity/pattern, prior withdrawal/seizure, last drink, nutrition, medications/substances, depression/suicide risk and liver-decompensation symptoms.
workup: Assess CBC/chemistry/liver/synthetic function and fibrosis/decompensation as indicated plus alternative liver causes.
Evaluate infection/bleeding/renal injury urgently in decompensated disease.
management: Treat withdrawal safely when present, correct nutrition/thiamine risk and manage liver complications according to severity.
Offer evidence-based AUD pharmacotherapy/psychosocial treatment with liver-specific medication selection and addiction supports.
medicationSafety: Medication for AUD must account for hepatic/renal disease and interactions; avoid assuming every approved medication is equally suitable in decompensated cirrhosis.
Sedatives for withdrawal require protocolized monitoring, especially with encephalopathy/respiratory risk.
counselling: Use person-first language and frame abstinence/reduction treatment as medical care, not a moral test.
Discuss transplant/addiction pathways when advanced disease is present without prejudging eligibility.
followUp: Close the loop on addiction treatment, liver staging, vaccination, nutrition and cirrhosis surveillance/complications.
examTrap: Telling a jaundiced patient simply to stop alcohol and return later without assessing withdrawal risk or decompensated liver disease.
oneLinePearl: Treat the liver disease and the alcohol use disorder at the same visit.
sourceBasis: Canadian alcohol use disorder guideline resources
Canadian hepatology alcohol-related liver disease practice principles
